articles.text: The supreme court of Dakota adjourned Tuesday, at Deadwood, to meet in Bismarck Nov. 14.
articles.summary: The Dakota supreme court adjourned at Deadwood on Tuesday, to meet next in Bismarck on November 14.

articles.text: Captain Dan. Maratta has been appointed United States Marshal of Dakota to take the place of General Allen. All who know the new Marshal recommend him highly and look for a "clean-up" of some of the rottenness that has disgraced Dakota.
articles.summary: Captain Dan Maratta has been appointed U.S. Marshal of Dakota, succeeding General Allen.

articles.text: No progress seems to have been made by the men who are trying to "civil service" Governor Pierce out of office. For the sake of honest government, cleanness in politics and the good name of Dakota, it is to be hoped that in this instance at least, there will be no change.
articles.summary: The paper hopes efforts to remove Dakota Governor Pierce from office will fail.

articles.text: Riel has again been repreived by the English government. We doubt if any one man has ever been a greater white elephant to Canada and even to England, than Riel is proving to be. Canada put her foot into it badly by not in the first place granting some or all of the half-breeds' requests and is now suffering the just retribution she deserves. Canada has too near a neighbor in the United States not to adopt a liberal policy with all her citizens.
articles.summary: Editorial on Louis Riel's latest reprieve, blaming Canada's handling of the half-breeds' requests.

articles.text: The Republicans carried Ohio Tuesday by about 20,000 majority. This shows a Republican gain over 1883 of about 25,000. The Prohibitionists did not materially change the result. The next legislature will be Republican, which insures the re-election to the Senate of the old war-horse, John Sherman. A queer anomaly of the contest was that the Prohibitionists joined the liquor interest in an attempt to down the Republicans, by which party alone they can ever expect to have any of their cranky notions carried out. Politics makes queer bed fellows.
articles.summary: Comment on the Republican victory in Ohio's Tuesday election, ensuring John Sherman's re-election.

articles.text: Chief Justice Edgerton sends his resignation to Washington and will enter the senatorial race against Judge Moody of Deadwood. To a man up a tree this looks as though Judge Edgerton had abandoned a very plump bird in the hahd for a very poor one in the bush. There is no state as yet and no real likelihood of there being one, of which he can become senator and the chances are few of his beating such an accomplished wire puller as Judge Moody in the senatorial or any other race. Bartlett Tripp is taking Judge Edgerton's resignation to Washington, with a good chance of being appointed in his stead.
articles.summary: Chief Justice Edgerton has resigned to run for senator against Judge Moody; Bartlett Tripp carries the resignation to Washington and may succeed him.

articles.text: It looks as though the Northern Pacific rail road and the Montana Improvement Co. would have to pay handsomely for the wood they have cut from government land. M. J. Haley, special timber agent, has made his reports to Washington, which include thirty-one separate indictments against the above companies for a gross amount of $613,402. Mr. Haley is especially denunciatory of the Montana Improvement Co., calling it an "unscrupulous organization that will leave nothing undone to gain its point." The Improvement Co. cut the most or all of the timber, but the rail road company is implicated as it held a controlling interest in its stock.
articles.summary: Special timber agent M. J. Haley has reported thirty-one indictments totaling $613,402 against the Northern Pacific and the Montana Improvement Co. for timber cut on government land.

articles.headline: Mud-slinging.
articles.text:
The mistakes of the eastern press in reference to the range cattle business would be amusing were it not for the fact that in many instances they are unjust and damaging. They are also gradually leading eastern public opinion into the belief that the "cattle kings" are in all cases interlopers and that in some way people in the east suffer a personal loss for the money made in the range cattle business.

The true facts in the case are so apparent that it seems strange eastern papers have not manhood enough to publish them. In a nut-shell, the country occupied by the range cattle business would be entirely uninhabited, were it not for this industry. We doubt if a case has ever occured where range cattle business has crowded out agriculture. On the other hand, in Texas, Colorado, Kansas and other states and territories, agriculture is constantly restricting the bounds of the cattle business. These facts are so apparent that they scarcely need mention. As fast as the range country is needed for agriculture, as much as is fit for that pursuit will be given over to it.

Thus far only is the cattleman an interloper. He makes profitable a country that without him would be a howling wilderness and as soon as he has established a market the farmer comes in, with no opposition from the stockman, chooses the best hundred and sixty acres he can find and goes to farming.

All this cry about there being need of laws to allow farmers to settle up range territory is the purest cant. There isn't a range in the United States, not absolutely owned by the ranchman, upon which the settler cannot come and establish a farm. The laws of the United States would uphold him in it and if the venom-slingers of the east knew as much about land laws as they do about penny-a-line mud throwing they would see that attempts to arouse public opinion against cattlemen for keeping out farmers were built on a foundation of sand.

Another howl the eastern press is raising is: "Why don't the cattlemen buy the land?" If these editors knew what they were talking about, they would see what a boomerang their question is. How can one man legally get posession of more land than a homestead, pre-emption and tree-claim will give him and how far will this go in pasturing even a small bunch of cattle.

Time and again, in the Chicago meeting of 1884, of the National Cattle growers' Association, in the Wyoming association meeting of 1885 and by many other associations, have attempts been made to get Congress to pass laws, leasing the land to cattlemen at a reasonable figure. These attempts are disregarded, however by eastern editors, who bid fair, either through ignorance or sheer spite-work, to arouse a sentiment in the east that may fall with crushing force on the way of legislation, on the range cattle business.
articles.summary: Editorial defending the range cattle business against eastern press charges that cattlemen are interlopers keeping out farmers, and urging land-leasing legislation.

articles.text: S. E. Grindall, of Beaver creek, has been appointed deputy sheriff by sheriff Tuttle of Glendive. We congratulate Mr. Grindall, and also Mr. Tuttle for securing such an efficient deputy, but it would turn out somewhat of a joke if Mr. Grindall was found to live in Billings Co., Dakota.
articles.summary: S. E. Grindall of Beaver creek has been appointed deputy sheriff by Sheriff Tuttle of Glendive, though he may actually live in Billings County, Dakota.

articles.text: Mr. John H. Obery, the Superintendent of Indian schools, under Secretary Lamar, gave his idea of the Indian question at the Lake Mahonk, N. Y., Indian Civilization Conference last Friday. We might also add that he gave himself dead away on the same occasion. In speaking of the education of Indians, he says: "After educating the boys I would suggest teaching them cattle raising, allowing them to contract with white men to take herds on their reservations and return them when called for, all the work on the reservations to be done by Indians. I would also favor assisting them to raise cattle for themselves." Mr. Obery said in conclusion: "I hope to make some radical changes, for I believe that only through the school-house can the Indian be let into the light of civilization." We were going to make some comments on the above extract, but hope we have no such tenderfoot among our readers that it is needed. We wonder though, that it did not occur to Mr. Obery, that it would be a good plan to first educate the cattlemen into allowing the Indians to take care of their cattle. This is an avenue of wealth that the cowman has hitherto not seemed to grasp.
articles.summary: Sarcastic comment on Indian schools superintendent John H. Obery's proposal at the Lake Mohonk conference that Indians herd white men's cattle on reservations.

articles.text: Our market report shows a great improvement in the price of northern range cattle, the highest quotation raising 40c., to $5.00. The receipts of cattle in Chicago, averaged 7,237 per day last week, against 7,523 per day for the preceding week. New York prices ruled 30@50c. higher and English prices were generally lower. All desirable grades of cattle were in brisk demand at Chicago and prices were about 25c. higher all through. Some good Montana rangers sold at $5.10. All range cattle were in better condition than heretofore.
articles.summary: Northern range cattle prices improved in Chicago, with the top quotation up 40 cents to $5.00.

articles.text: Two cars each of VI and SOHO cattle were shipped from Mingusville last Friday. Charlie Eaton went with them to Chicago.
articles.summary: Two cars each of VI and SOHO cattle were shipped from Mingusville last Friday, with Charlie Eaton accompanying them to Chicago.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific is doing a land-office business shipping cattle. Last night, five full stock trains came through and as many more are expected this afternoon. They all come from Glendive and Billings.
articles.summary: Five full stock trains from Glendive and Billings came through last night, with as many more expected.

articles.text: Osborne Bros. suffered another loss at their Æ ranch, on Andrew's creek, not long since. Their range was completely burned over, necessitating the removal of their cattle, the building of a new shack and the putting up of another supply of hay. The loss is not irreparable, but will make plenty of hard work before winter.
articles.summary: Fire burned over the Osborne Bros.' range at their Æ ranch on Andrew's creek, forcing them to move cattle, build a new shack and put up more hay.

articles.text: J. W. Buster came down from the Hashknife camp yesterday, and this morning delivered 507 beeves to the Ref. Car Co., averaging 1113 pounds.
articles.summary: J. W. Buster of the Hashknife camp delivered 507 beeves averaging 1113 pounds to the Refrigerator Car Co.

articles.text: Oh, but won't there be a picnic in Southern Dakota if that half should by any chance be admitted. You can't throw a club down there without hitting a disgruntled sore-head politician of the east who has come to Dakota in search of official pap and has waited lo, these many years for it. It will almost turn out like some women's conventions where each [one?] [votes?] for herself for every office.
articles.summary: Jab at office-seeking politicians in southern Dakota should that half be admitted as a state.

articles.text: Speaking of their quality, Mr. Gray of Canada says: "Of all the ox-kings, I have found the Aberdeen-Angus to be the best feeders. They respond the quickest to rich, concentrated food, and when they are in the stalls they are the most contented cattle I have ever tried. When the Aberdeen's stomach is filled, he lies down and rests. Of them, says Mr. Leonard, of Bell Air, Mo., who has imported, bought and sold more of them than any other man: "I can load a Burton car with Angus cattle at New York, carry them across the continent and back again, and have them gain flesh every day on the journey."—[Montana Stock Gazette.
articles.summary: Reprinted praise of Aberdeen-Angus cattle as feeders, from the Montana Stock Gazette.

articles.headline: Stock Terms.
articles.text:
As there is often a mixing up of the use of terms used by breeders, the following, from a manual on cattle, may serve to give our readers a proper idea as to their meaning:

A breed is a race, class or kind of animals, having certain peculiarities of form, and other characteristics different from others of the some species.

Thoroughbred animals are those which have been bred in a direct line sufficiently long to establish a fixed type, which they have the power of transmitting with uniformity to their offspring.

Cross-bred animals are the offspring of a thoroughbred male of one breed out of a female of another breed.

Grades are the offspring of a thoroughbred male or female and what are known as common stock, which belongs to no particular breed, or any other thorough or cross-breed.

High grades are those having a preponderance of pure blood, such as the offspring of a thoroughbred bull out of a half-bred cow, which is three-fourths.

Low grades embrace half-breeds and all graduations below so long as the impress of the thoroughbred is visible.

Common stock, scrubs, or natives, are those which have been indiscriminately bred until there is no recognizable trace of any breed and no uniformity of type.—[Farm Journal.

The above will be found interesting but in the definition of "Thoroughbred" we believe misleading. Although considerable license is now used in this meaning, the word "Thoroughbred" refers only to horses that can be traced back to an Arabian origin. "Thoroughbred" as applied to cattle is strictly a mis-nomer, "full-blood" being the term to use. Consequently the word "thoroughbred" in the above definitions should be changed to "full-blood." We publish the article as it is being widely copied, in order that this distinction may be recognized. It might be admissable in conversation, to speak of a thoroughbred heifer as one's meaning can be easily understood, but in the printed definitions, it is necessary to be exact.
articles.summary: Definitions of cattle-breeding terms from the Farm Journal, with an editorial note that 'full-blood' rather than 'thoroughbred' is correct for cattle.

articles.text: A close observing horseman gives the following rules and marks for determining a horse's age: "At one year the colt has a full set of temporary front teeth, which are short, round and very white. At the age of two the colt sheds two center front teeth, above and below, and the horse teeth make their appearance. At three four others are lost, one on each side of the first. At four the corner teeth drop out. At the age of five the new horse teeth at the corners are up even with the others, the mouth is full and the tusks appear. At five the cavities or cups in the center will be nearly worn away and the tusks are up full, white and sharp. At seven the cups disappear from the front middle teeth, being brown curved lines. At eight the cups are all out save the corner ones. At nine the teeth are all full, shut even, and present a fair appearance. At ten the teeth turn yellow or brown, the tusks are either blunt or very long, the gums shrink away, giving the teeth a very large appearance. At eleven the teeth are black and foul, the gums form points between them. At twelve the upper teeth begin to overhang the lower ones. At thirteen the front teeth thicken and assume a triangular shape. A horse has forty teeth; twenty-four grinders, four tusks and twelve incisors or nippers. The colt is born with eight double teeth; at about two months four more appear, one upon each jaw. At one four more come, and at the age of two four others, and at three four more, making the mouth full, twenty-four grinders.—[Ex.
articles.summary: Reprinted rules for telling a horse's age by its teeth.

articles.summary: Indians off the Berthold agency killed seven elk down the river.

articles.text: Charlie Eaton, after delivering the VI and SOHO cattle in Chicago, will visit in Pittsburgh, his old home.
articles.summary: Charlie Eaton will visit his old home of Pittsburgh after delivering VI and SOHO cattle in Chicago.

articles.text: The Metropolitan hotel will receive a house-warming to-night, in the shape of a dance, given by the new landlord, J. B. Walker. All are invited.
articles.summary: The Metropolitan hotel's new landlord J. B. Walker gives a house-warming dance to-night.

articles.text: Mr. Hostetter of Pittsburgh, Pa., who makes an annual pilgrimage to the Bad Lands, is now visiting at Howard Eaton's ranch.
articles.summary: Mr. Hostetter of Pittsburgh is making his annual Bad Lands visit at Howard Eaton's ranch.

articles.text: The bridge two miles west of Andrew's burned out last night, catching fire from sparks from an ash-pan. The evening passenger was delayed about four hours.
articles.summary: A railroad bridge two miles west of Andrew's burned last night from ash-pan sparks, delaying the evening passenger about four hours.

articles.text: E. Kessler of New York, returned home last Monday, after a month's hunting at Jack McGregor's ranch. He had moderately good luck, securing several fine heads.
articles.summary: E. Kessler of New York went home Monday after a month's hunting at Jack McGregor's ranch.

articles.text: Messrs. Allan and Walker, who made a short visit here to look at the wonders of the Bad Lands, recently "reciprocated" to Judge Gordon, by sending him a box of fine cigars from their home in Warren, Pa.
articles.summary: Recent visitors Allan and Walker of Warren, Pa., sent Judge Gordon a box of cigars.

articles.text: Dr. Heber Robarts came from Dickinson, Monday, to attend Mrs. O'Hara, who had injured herself about the head in falling from a chair on which she had been standing. The patient has nearly recovered.
articles.summary: Dr. Heber Robarts came from Dickinson to treat Mrs. O'Hara for a head injury from a fall.

articles.text: The side-track to the new stock-yards is nearly laid and the work on the yards themselves will be finished in a few days. The work is superintended by Messrs. Thayer and Travelpiece, who are rushing it through both well and quickly.
articles.summary: The side-track to the new stock-yards is nearly laid and the yards will soon be finished under Thayer and Travelpiece.

articles.summary: List of arrivals by Northern Pacific during the past week.

articles.text: Mrs. James Harmon returned last week from her visit to Minnesota, where she has been visiting for several months. During her absence, the Harmon family was increased by a brand-new girl baby, which Jim declares is "the chief."
articles.summary: Mrs. James Harmon returned from several months in Minnesota, where a baby girl was born to the Harmons.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts has completed his contract of grading for the stock-yards and started this morning for Rapid City, to deliver the buffalo, bought here. The purchasers also bought a buffalo bull calf in Miles City, which Lloyd will take in a wagon.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts finished grading for the stock-yards and left for Rapid City to deliver the buffalo sold here, plus a bull calf from Miles City.

articles.text: Several persons are making preparations to hunt for the market during the coming season. We doubt if there will be anything more than a living in it for good hunters, as deer are scarcer than usual and owing to the immense territory tributary to the St. Paul market, prices will be as low as they were last season.
articles.summary: Several men plan to market-hunt this season, though deer are scarce and St. Paul prices low.

articles.text: E. Kessler and Tommy McGregor, while hunting below the mouth of Beaver, came upon two bears feeding. The former carried a rifle, while Tommy had a shot-gun. Mr. Kessler hadn't lost any bear and refused either to shoot or allow Tommy to use his rifle. As trees were not very handy, it was, perhaps a wise move, though Tommy even yet regrets that he did not turn loose with No. 6 shot.
articles.summary: E. Kessler and Tommy McGregor met two bears below the mouth of Beaver creek but declined to shoot.

articles.text: The most of the outfits north of the track dropped out of the round-up when it reached Mingusville. Their places were more than filled by the outfits south of the track. The round-up is making rapid headway and will probably be back at Medora inside of a week. The cattle are in good fix and unless something unforeseen turns up, will pass through the winter with even less loss than there was last winter.
articles.summary: Northern outfits left the round-up at Mingusville, replaced by southern outfits; the round-up should reach Medora within a week and cattle are in good condition.

articles.text: We stated incidentally once that the coal-bank at Mattox' ranch, on the old tie road, was about forty feet thick in sight and extended an unknown distance below the bed of Deep creek, on which it is located. We couldn't at the time have imbibed enough Dakota ozone as Mrs. Mattox has measured the vein and declares it is sixty feet in height from the top of the vein to the water in the stream. Western Dakota ought not to suffer with cold as long as it its foundation consists of such strata of coal.
articles.summary: Mrs. Mattox measured the coal vein at Mattox' ranch on Deep creek at sixty feet.

articles.headline: Pen-itential Musings.
articles.text:
It is hard to tell where the poetical muse will sometimes strike, and we publish the following self-explanatory verse on account of its authorship. Every local reader of the Cow Boy can give a good guess as to its origin:

To J. H.—
I lushed up and went on a racket,
Billy Smith, he gave me a steer,
They brought me before Judge Coburn,
Who immediately gave me five year.
He saw that my health was fast failing,
And mentioned the same there and then,
But he told me to get ready for calling
And go visit the boys in the pen.
I was met at the gate by the warden,
Who told me to banish my gloom,
For although the hotel was quite crowded,
He could manage to find me a room.
So they washed me, they clipped me, they shaved me,
They gave me a suit to begin,
Two blankets, a pillow and bucket,
And I commenced to keep rooms in the pen.
We get breakfast at six in the morning,
At seven we go on parade,
Our style is so grand and imposing,
It would rival the Irish brigade.
Corporal Conly then gave his orders:
"Keep step there, and close up, my men!
Or I'll skull drag you bold seventh warders
And banish you all from the pen."
We walk out in line in the morning,
And immediately go to our work,
And I pity the fellow caught talking,
Or the poor devil who offers to shirk.
You can show this to all of the boys,
And if you have a dear friend,
Just tell him to keep clear of Montana,
If he wants to keep out of the pen.
W. R.
articles.summary: Verse signed 'W. R.' from a Montana penitentiary inmate, addressed to 'J. H.', which the paper says local readers will recognize.
